content: There has been a significant reduction in the incidence and prevalence of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) among young children in regions where universal infant vaccination programs have been implemented. Target groups for catch-up vaccination and other preventive strategies include young adolescents, household and sexual contacts of individuals who are HBsAg-positive, and individuals at high risk of acquiring HBV infection, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), and individuals with multiple sexual partners. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of antiviral agents, such as tenofovir and entecavir, for the treatment of hepatitis B infection. These agents are effective in suppressing HBV replication, preventing progression to cirrhosis, and reducing the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and liver-related deaths. However, individuals with replicating virus may require lifelong treatment. Recent analyses of global hepatitis C virus (HCV) prevalence suggest that fewer people are living with HCV infection than previously estimated. Approximately 80 million individuals have chronic viremic HCV infection. Despite declining incidence, many individuals infected 30–60 years ago are now succumbing to HCV-related cirrhosis and liver cancer, as these complications often take decades to develop. According to the Global Burden of Disease study, deaths due to HCV increased from 333,000 in 1990 to 704,000 in 2013, and this trend is projected to continue unless treatment is significantly scaled up. HIV and HCV share common transmission routes, and individuals with HIV, particularly PWID and MSM, are at increased risk of HCV infection. With the widespread use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) reducing HIV-associated opportunistic infections, HCV-related liver disease has become a leading cause of death among people living with HIV in some high-income countries. HCV is primarily transmitted through healthcare-associated procedures, injecting drug use, mother-to-child transmission (MTCT), and sexual contact. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), HCV infection is often linked to unsafe injection practices and inadequate infection control in healthcare settings. In high-income countries, most HCV infections occur among individuals who use unsterile equipment to inject drugs. PWID have a high global prevalence of HCV infection, estimated at around 67%. MTCT of HCV occurs at a moderate rate, with higher risk in HIV-co-infected mothers. Sexual transmission of HCV is more common among HIV-positive individuals, particularly MSM, but is rare among HIV-negative heterosexual couples. The natural history of HCV infection involves both acute and chronic phases. Acute HCV infection is defined by the presence of HCV RNA, core antigen, and antibodies within six months of exposure. Most acute infections are asymptomatic, and spontaneous clearance occurs in 15–45% of cases within six months. Chronic HCV infection develops in the remaining 55–85% of individuals and can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, and HCC. The risk of cirrhosis is 15–30% within 20 years, and the annual risk of HCC in individuals with cirrhosis is approximately 2–4%. Diagnosis of HCV infection involves initial serological screening for evidence of past or current infection, followed by nucleic acid testing (NAT) to confirm active infection. Clearance of HCV, whether spontaneous or treatment-induced, does not provide immunity against reinfection. Prevention of HCV infection relies on reducing exposure to the virus, as no vaccine is currently available. WHO guidelines emphasize infection control in healthcare settings and screening of blood products. Harm reduction strategies, such as providing sterile injecting equipment, are critical for preventing HCV transmission among PWID. The advent of direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) has revolutionized HCV treatment, offering short-duration regimens with cure rates exceeding 90% and fewer adverse effects compared to older interferon-based therapies. WHO updated its HCV treatment guidelines in 2016 to include recommendations for DAAs. The development of pangenotypic DAAs will eliminate the need for genotype testing, further expanding access to treatment. Serological assays are commonly used for initial screening due to their low cost and ability to detect host immune responses or viral antigens. NAT technologies are used to confirm active infection, guide treatment decisions, and assess virological cure or suppression. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) provide quick, qualitative results and are particularly useful in settings with limited laboratory infrastructure.
